newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Will post-97 Hong Kong ruin the environment.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Will post-97 Hong Kong ruin the environment.

text.p: In a city where money is king, land is mainly a place to put buildings and the sea is a dumping site for raw sewage, Hong Kong's green groups have been chipping away at society's indifference towards the environment.
Now environmentalists are looking to Hong Kong's handover to China, where some of the world's worst ecological degradation is taking place, with a mixture of trepidation -- and hope.
Hong Kong becomes a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China on July 1 after more than 150 years as a British colony.

In that time the tiny territory has gone from a sleepy backwater of green hills and crystal clear bays to a capitalist powerhouse of gleaming office towers, surging stock prices and ever-growing mounds of garbage.
"People say Hong Kong has a first-class economy and a third-class environment," said Alex Yau, senior conservation officer at World Wide Fund for Nature Hong Kong (WWF).

There has never been much doubt China will do its best to nurture Hong Kong's first class economy. What remains to be seen is whether the change from British colony to Chinese SAR will help or hinder efforts to upgrade the third-class environment.
FOCUS ON ECONOMY MAY ERODE GREEN AWARENESS

While activists in the West may chain themselves to trees or lay down in front of bulldozers in efforts to curb development, Hong Kong environmentalists tend to sit on government-appointed panels to discuss options with developers and officials.

The WWF's Yau said working within the system, while not always effective, has put environmental concerns on the agenda of both government and business policy makers -- no mean feat in a city that worships unfettered, laissez faire capitalist development.
But there is concern that nascent ecological awareness could fade after Hong Kong's handover, especially with the prospect of a post-handover local administration dominated by businessmen.
SAR Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa, a millionaire former shipping tycoon, has said little about the environment, but has made clear that his top priority is the economy.
"It is only through sustained economic growth that we might create more wealth and resources to improve the quality of life for Hong Kong people," Tung said in a recent speech.
It took green groups four months of lobbying before they managed to get a meeting with Tung last month. Then, when they met, nothing much came out of it.

"Mr Tung acknowledged the need to protect the environment so that Hong Kong can attract the best people to live and work here," Friends of the Earth (FoE) director Mei Ng said after the meeting. "In the end, there was little green commitment."

Also worrying is Beijing's replacement of Hong Kong's elected legislature with a council chosen by a China-backed committee. As a result, half of the legislature's environmental affairs panel will be out of office come July 1.

With fewer legislative advocates and uncertain executive interest, there are concerns that environmental progress may be stalled. But many environmentalists actually hope the handover will be a unique chance to help Hong Kong's environment.
HANDOVER MAY PROMPT REVIEW OF ENVIRONMENT POLICIES

"I think actually the handover is a very good opportunity to revisit the whole thing rather than remaining in a very bureaucratic approach and just looking to the next step, and I think he (Tung) is trying to do that," said Yau.
Tung, because he comes from business rather than from government, is not so tied to past government policies and may be better placed to fully review options, she said.

"The thing I like most is that his approach is somewhat visionary -- he doesn't say we have this or that system, he tries to see ahead and say what do we want Hong Kong to be in the 21st century," Yau said.

Green groups also hope Hong Kong will have better cooperation with Chinese officials after the handover on environmental policy, which would no longer be held hostage to repeated flare ups in Sino-British political relations.
This is especially crucial as pollution in China worsenS and affects Hong Kong to a greater extent in the future.
Hong Kong people themselves may also feel different about their home after the handover, many green activists say.

The territory is called a "borrowed place, borrowed time", a British colony populated by refugees from other parts of China, where everybody felt transient. After the handover, people may feel more at home and treat it as such, activists hope.

On a more practical level, the WWF's Yau said many people are focused on making money as security against uncertainty ahead of the handover. Once it is past, more people may be ready to pay attention to other issues, like the environment, she said.
GROWING POPULATION STRAINS TINY TERRITORY

With 6.4 people crammed into 1,095 square kilometres of land, it is a wonder that there is any green left in Hong Kong, but in fact just a few steps behind many a high-rise apartment block are verdant hills and cool valleys.
Hong Kong also boasts the Mai Po marshes, one of the world's richest habitats for waterfowl, and the sea around Hong Kong is home to the rare and endangered Chinese pink dolphins.
But for most people, Hong Kong is a place to make money, and government policymaking has focused on feeding, housing and keeping employed a population growing in size and aspirations.

Gross domestic product (GDP) growth has averaged 6.5 percent annually for 10 years, hitting US$24,500 a head this year, but raw sewage still pours into Hong Kong's "fragrant" harbour and rising tides of smog obscure the famous waterfront view.
China has promised Hong Kong people will rule Hong Kong after the handover. Environmentalists hope that also means Hong Kong people will be more responsible about Hong Kong's environment.
"Is the environment a priority for the new SAR leadership? I hate to say it, but perhaps only time will tell," said the FoE's Mei Ng.
